constraint: CPU core count, device memory and GPU renderer must together describe a configuration the vendor actually ships. Each field being individually legal is not sufficient.

evidence.source: capture differential: an 8-core / 16GB machine reporting an Apple Max-tier GPU. Max silicon ships at 14+ cores and 36GB minimum, so the combination is not purchasable.

evidence.note: deviceMemory rounds physical RAM to a power of two and clamps to [2,32] on desktop, so it constrains installed RAM to a range rather than naming it

notes: The characteristic failure of per-field synthesis. Replaying a real capture cannot produce it.

constraint: The GPU named by WebGL and the GPU described by WebGPU's adapter limits, architecture and feature set must be the same device.

evidence.source: capture differential: WebGL renderer changed to a newer GPU while every WebGPU adapter limit stayed byte-identical to the real hardware and architecture still read metal-3

notes: WebGPU is the second emitter most likely to be forgotten; see docs/SUBSYSTEMS.md.

constraint: The renderer string in GPUInfo and the one WebGL returns must agree.

evidence.note: GPUInfo path, GPU process
reads GL_RENDERER live through the command buffer; this is what JavaScript sees

notes: Two independent emitters. Patching only the GPUInfo one changes chrome://gpu and leaves every detector's value untouched.

constraint: Every render surface must return byte-identical output across repeated reads within a session.

evidence.source: own capture, real Chrome 152 on M4 Max: canvas, WebGL1, WebGL2 and the audio render byte-identical across two separate page loads

notes: Axiom A3 measured rather than asserted. Per-call noise violates this by construction.

constraint: An element's reported rect must agree with its computed style. Where computed style declares integer CSS coordinates, getBoundingClientRect must return exactly those coordinates; a sub-pixel offset against an integer declaration cannot arise naturally.
check: rect.x == computed.left and rect.y == computed.top for integer-positioned elements

evidence.source: own capture: real Chrome returns x=-10000, y=0 for an element at left:-10000px; top:0
capture differential: a perturbing browser returned x=-10000.015625, y=-0.03125 for the same stylesheet — offsets of 1/64 and 1/32 px

notes: Geometry noise is more identifying than the value it hides: the artifact has no natural cause.

constraint: The OS named by the UA string, navigator.platform, userAgentData and the Sec-CH-UA-Platform header must be the same OS.

evidence.source: own capture: all four agree in stock Chrome

constraint: The browser major version in the UA string, in userAgentData brands and fullVersionList, and in the Sec-CH-UA header must match. Brand list order and the GREASE entry are randomised by the engine and are not part of the constraint.

evidence.source: own capture and capture differential: both browsers were internally consistent here; order and GREASE punctuation differed between them and both are legitimate

notes: Do not treat brand order or the GREASE brand as a tell — Chrome varies both deliberately.

constraint: The difference between screen and available dimensions must be plausible window furniture for the claimed OS. The exact inset varies with dock and menu bar state and cannot be pinned to a single value.

evidence.source: own capture: 1728x1117 screen, 1728x1001 available — a 116px inset from macOS menu bar and dock
two captures of one MacBook five hours apart
evidence.note: availHeight was 1001 in one session and 1003 in the other, so the inset varies with dock state and an exact value cannot be required — only a plausible one

notes: Measured variance on real hardware is why this is a plausibility constraint rather than an equality one.

constraint: Installed fonts, speech synthesis voices, system colours and system fonts must all belong to the claimed OS.

evidence.source: own capture: 32 fonts detected and 86-entry voice list, both macOS-specific

notes: Four surfaces, one cause. Cheap to get right when the host OS matches the claim and very hard when it does not.

constraint: Timezone must be identical on the main thread, in workers, and in the browser process.
notes: Three override layers. Setting one leaves contexts disagreeing about what time it is, detectable by comparing a Date in a worker against one on the main thread.

constraint: The reported timezone must be plausible for the geographic location of the connection's exit IP.

evidence.source: follows from the claim being a whole device on a network, not two independent settings

notes: Jointly owned by subsystems 8 and 10; held by the arbiter rather than either shard.

constraint: WebRTC ICE candidates must agree with the claimed network position and must not reveal a host address inconsistent with it.

evidence.note: kWebRTCIPHandlingPolicy

notes: Jointly owned by subsystems 9 and 10.

constraint: Against an origin advertising HTTP/3, the browser must attempt QUIC wherever stock Chrome would, including when a proxy is configured.

evidence.note: QUIC is attempted only when proxy_info_.is_direct(), so a proxied session silently loses HTTP/3

notes: Why SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE is a coherence requirement rather than a feature. See docs/subsystems/network-proxy.md.

constraint: The Device-Memory client hint header and navigator.deviceMemory must report the same value.

evidence.note: the same static is computed independently in the browser and renderer processes, so they can disagree
header and JavaScript value agree in both cases, including when the claim is rounded away from the requested figure

notes: Cheap for a server to check and impossible to notice from inside the renderer.

constraint: A profile should claim resources at or below what the host can satisfy. Claiming more is permitted but carries weak-evidence risk, because measured parallelism plateaus at the host's real capacity.

evidence.note: thread pools size from NumberOfProcessors, so a worker scaling curve plateaus at the host's real core count whatever the reported value says

NumberOfProcessors narrows by the CPU affinity mask on Linux but has no CFS-quota handling, so a --cpuset-cpus container reports correctly while a --cpus container over-reports — the contradiction needs quota limits, load or throttling rather than any container

notes: Weak, not fatal. A scaling-curve probe fires on containerized, virtualized, loaded and throttled real browsers alike, so no detector can rule on it. The loader clamps and warns rather than refusing: trading a rarely-probed weak signal for a hard usability failure is the worse deal. Only two fields are host-coupled; device identity is portable.

constraint: A session configured through a proxy must remain proxied across network changes. No transport may reconnect directly to the origin.

evidence.note: Migrate() reconnects to connection()->peer_address(), so a peer address set to the origin rather than the SOCKS relay would open a direct socket to the origin on every network change

notes: Not a fingerprinting edge but a leak: the failure is silent, only occurs on network transition, and deproxies the session including the real client address. Settled in docs/subsystems/network-proxy.md by requiring the QUIC peer address to be the relay.

constraint: A canvas of flat fills must encode to approximately the size real rendering produces. Per-pixel perturbation destroys the run-length structure PNG relies on, so the encoded length inflates even though every individual pixel remains plausible.
check: len(toDataURL(flat_fill_canvas)) within expected range for the drawn content

evidence.note: a 60x30 single-colour fill encoded to 262 bytes in stock Chrome and 406 in a browser injecting canvas noise — 55% larger for identical drawing commands

notes: A passive check costing one canvas draw and a string length, needing no pixel comparison and no reference value. It detects the presence of noise rather than the identity of the device, which is why axiom A3 forbids noise outright instead of trying to make it subtle.

constraint: TextMetrics values must carry the precision real rasterisation produces. Ascent and descent at common font sizes land on exact values; a near-integer with a long fractional tail indicates a perturbed measurement rather than a measured one.
check: measureText fields match the reference exactly, including their precision

evidence.note: stock Chrome returned fontBoundingBoxAscent 13 and actualBoundingBoxAscent 15; a perturbing browser returned 13.00003373571476 and 15.000038925824724 for the same string and font

notes: Same failure as coh.layout-integer-positions in a different API: the perturbation is more identifying than the value it conceals.

constraint: Every high-entropy client hint delivered as a request header must equal the same value read from navigator.userAgentData.getHighEntropyValues() in the page it was sent for.
check: all(header['sec-ch-ua-'+h] == uaData.high[h] for h in high_entropy_hints)

evidence.note: one GetUserAgentMetadata call in the browser feeds the header path and, by mojo copy, the JS path — so in stock Chrome they cannot disagree, and any disagreement is introduced by us
two emission sites in two processes read that one struct; a patch applied at only one of them breaks this edge

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: all eight high-entropy values in probes['navigator.userAgentData'].high match their headers in probes['headers.echo'] exactly

notes: The client-hints analogue of coh.device-memory-header-vs-js, and cheaper for a server to check because it needs no JavaScript at all beyond one echo.

constraint: navigator.userAgentData.platform and the Sec-CH-UA-Platform header must be the same string.

evidence.note: both read metadata.platform from GetPlatformForUAMetadata

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: navigator.userAgentData.platform "macOS" and sec-ch-ua-platform "macOS"

notes: Split out from the general edge because Sec-CH-UA-Platform needs no Accept-CH opt-in: a server gets it on the very first request, before scripts run, so this pair is checkable on a bare page load.

constraint: The brand list in navigator.userAgentData.brands and the Sec-CH-UA header must contain the same brand/version pairs in the same order, including the GREASE entry.

evidence.note: the header is a structured-header serialisation of the same brand_version_list vector the JS accessor copies, so order is preserved rather than coincidental

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: brands [Chromium 152, Not?A_Brand 24, Google Chrome 152] and sec-ch-ua "Chromium";v="152", "Not?A_Brand";v="24", "Google Chrome";v="152" — same entries, same order

notes: Order is randomised across versions but not across surfaces within one browser. coh.ua-version-agreement correctly says order is not a tell when comparing two browsers; this edge says order must still be identical between the header and the JS value of the SAME browser, which is a different claim and does hold.

constraint: The brand-list permutation and the GREASE brand and version are deterministic functions of the claimed browser major version, so a profile claiming version N must present the list Chromium N would generate, not a list captured from a different version.

evidence.note: GetRandomOrder indexes a fixed permutation table by seed % 6 (or % 24), the GREASE brand picks punctuation by seed % 11 and (seed+1) % 11 from an 11-entry table, and the GREASE version is {"8","99","24"}[seed % 3] — the seed is the major version number, and no RNG is involved anywhere

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture, derived from source for seed=152: 152%11=9 gives '?', 153%11=10 gives '_', so "Not?A_Brand"; 152%3=2 gives "24"; 152%6=2 selects permutation {1,0,2} giving [Chromium, Not?A_Brand, Google Chrome]. The measured list is byte-identical to the derivation.

notes: Deliberately weak severity: this does NOT reintroduce brand order or GREASE as a detection signal, and coh.ua-version-agreement's rule that neither is a tell stands. It is a constraint on our own generator — the fields are not free parameters, so replaying a captured brand list beside a different claimed version manufactures a value stock Chrome never produces. A detector would need our source to spot it, which is why it is weak rather than fatal.

constraint: The Accept-Language request header and navigator.languages must describe the same ordered language list, allowing for the header's q-value expansion.

evidence.note: one pref, two independent transforms, delivered to two different processes — the renderer gets a bare comma list through RendererPreferences, the network service gets an expanded q-value string through GenerateAcceptLanguageHeader

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: Accept-Language "en-US,en;q=0.9" on the wire against navigator.languages ["en-US","en"]

notes: Structurally the same failure as coh.device-memory-header-vs-js and just as invisible from inside the renderer. Note the comparison must strip q-values and account for ExpandLanguageList adding base languages, so a naive string equality check produces false positives.

constraint: The navigator language list, the Accept-Language header and the locale resolved by Intl must name a consistent locale for the claimed device.

evidence.note: when the accept-languages pref is empty Blink falls back to Platform::Current()->DefaultLocale(), the host UI locale — so an unset profile value silently leaks the real machine locale into navigator.language

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: navigator.language "en-US", Accept-Language "en-US,en;q=0.9", Intl locale "en-US" — all agree while the timezone is Asia/Bangkok, which is a legitimate combination and must not be flagged

notes: Jointly owned with subsystem 8. Deliberately does not constrain locale against timezone: T0 shows a real device with en-US and Asia/Bangkok, so treating a locale/timezone mismatch as a tell would fire on real travellers and expatriates.

constraint: The User-Agent request header and navigator.userAgent must be byte-identical.

evidence.note: three writers in three processes, all reading embedder_support::GetUserAgent(); patching one leaves the others on the build's real string

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: the wire User-Agent and probes['navigator.scalars'].value.userAgent are identical strings

notes: The browser writes the navigation header before a renderer for that document exists, so a Blink-side patch cannot cover the first request even if it makes every later one agree.

constraint: navigator.appVersion must equal navigator.userAgent with the leading "Mozilla/" removed.

evidence.note: appVersion is agent.substr(agent.find('/') + 1); the relation holds by construction in stock Chrome and can only be broken by a patch

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: appVersion is exactly userAgent minus "Mozilla/"

notes: Cheap, decisive, and the classic casualty of a patch that overrides accessors one at a time instead of the emitter.

constraint: The mobile bit, the form-factor list and the presence of a "Mobile" token in the UA string must all describe the same class of device.
check: uaData.mobile == (header['sec-ch-ua-mobile'] == '?1') and form_factors == (['Mobile'] if uaData.mobile else ['Desktop']) and ('Mobile' in navigator.userAgent) == uaData.mobile

evidence.note: one switch, --use-mobile-user-agent, drives the mobile bit, the derived form-factor list and the " Mobile" product suffix; they are not independent fields

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: mobile false, form factors ["Desktop"], no "Mobile" token in the UA string

notes: Setting the mobile bit alone is never a complete change, and it also pulls in maxTouchPoints and screen geometry from subsystem 4.

constraint: The frozen engine constants must match the engine the UA string claims: a Chromium UA requires productSub "20030107" and vendor "Google Inc.".
check: navigator.productSub == '20030107' and navigator.vendor == 'Google Inc.' if 'Chrome/' in navigator.userAgent else True

evidence.note: both are literals; Gecko returns productSub "20100101" and an empty vendor, so the pair identifies the engine independently of the UA string

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: productSub "20030107", vendor "Google Inc." beside a Chrome/152 UA

notes: Free to satisfy by leaving both alone. Recorded because it is the check that catches a UA string edited without touching the engine.

constraint: navigator.pdfViewerEnabled must be true exactly when navigator.plugins holds the five spec-fixed PDF entries, and false exactly when it is empty.

evidence.note: the constructor fills the array only when IsPdfViewerAvailable() is true, and pdfViewerEnabled calls the same function — one bit, two observables, no intermediate state

evidence.source: own capture (resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json): own capture: pdfViewerEnabled true with the five-entry fixed plugin list

notes: Jointly relevant to subsystem 11. Any patch that fabricates a plugin list without going through this bit produces a combination the code cannot generate.

constraint: The UA string must not contain the "Headless" product token, and the brand list must contain the browser brand the UA claims.
check: 'Headless' not in navigator.userAgent and any(b.brand == claimed_brand for b in uaData.brands)

evidence.note: the --headless switch inserts "Headless" into the product token inside GetUserAgentInternal, upstream of every consumer, so it reaches the UA string, the header and appVersion together
the browser brand entry is compiled in only under #if !BUILDFLAG(CHROMIUM_BRANDING); a Chromium-branded build emits a two-entry brand list with no "Google Chrome", which no Chrome corpus row matches
brand is set only under #if !BUILDFLAG(CHROMIUM_BRANDING), so a Chromium build emits a brand list with no browser entry — a two-line patch, not a build blocker
GetUserAgentInternal inserts "Headless" into the product token when the --headless switch is present, upstream of every consumer

notes: Arbiter correction: the shard recorded both halves as build-configuration failures unreachable by an emitter patch. Both are reachable, and are now ordinary spoof rows. The brand entry is suppressed by an #if guard that a patch can simply drop, and the Headless token is inserted by a single command-line check in GetUserAgentInternal. Neither requires is_chrome_branded or src-internal. The edge itself stands as the invariant both patches must satisfy.

constraint: HDR is a single display property with four web-visible faces and they must agree: screen.colorDepth is 30 exactly when (color: 10) matches, exactly when (dynamic-range: high) matches, and — because an HDR colour space short-circuits the gamut computation to P3 — an HDR display can never report color-gamut srgb only. The SDR case is the mirror: colorDepth 24, (color: 8), dynamic-range standard only.
check: (colorDepth == 30) == (css.color == 10) == matchMedia('(dynamic-range: high)').matches and not (colorDepth == 30 and gamut == ['srgb'])

evidence.note: Display::SetDisplayColorSpacesRef derives color_depth and depth_per_component from color_spaces->SupportsHDR() — one input, two outputs
the platform sets 30/10 or 24/8 from the same enable_hdr boolean that installs the extended-sRGB output colour space
IsHDR() short-circuits the gamut to P3 before any primaries are examined
colorDepth 30, pixelDepth 30, color 10, dynamic-range ['standard','high'], color-gamut ['srgb','p3'] — all four faces of one HDR display, measured together

notes: Four surfaces, one cause, and the cheapest coherence check in this subsystem: three matchMedia calls and one property read. Any patch that writes screen.colorDepth without moving the display colour space fails it immediately. Also couples to the GPU subsystem — render_widget_host_impl.cc:1063-1069 strips HDR when hardware acceleration is off, so an HDR profile and software rendering are mutually exclusive.

constraint: The DPR client hint on the navigation request, the DPR client hint on subresource requests, window.devicePixelRatio and the CSS resolution media feature must all report the same ratio.

evidence.note: the navigation header is computed in the browser process from its own display list and host zoom map, with no renderer involvement
the subresource header is computed in the renderer from LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio, the same function window.devicePixelRatio forwards to
dpr: 2 on the wire against window.devicePixelRatio 2 in stock Chrome

notes: The direct analogue of coh.device-memory-header-vs-js, and the reason this subsystem's device scale factor patch has to land in the browser process. Note the two producers already differ in stock Chrome on a multi-monitor host, because the browser uses the primary display and the renderer uses the window's display — so the edge is only reliably checkable for a single-display profile, which is the case the corpus covers.

constraint: window.devicePixelRatio and the CSS resolution / -webkit-device-pixel-ratio media features must return the same number to full float precision, and both must scale with page zoom.

evidence.note: both are one-line forwarders to LocalFrame::DevicePixelRatio, so in stock Chrome they cannot disagree
the shared value is device_scale_factor x page zoom x css zoom, so it is not constant across zoom levels

notes: Zero-cost for a detector: a binary search over (min-resolution: Xdppx) recovers the float without reading the property, so wrapping or hiding window.devicePixelRatio accomplishes nothing. The second half of the constraint matters as much as the first — a patch that returns a fixed number makes the ratio stop responding to zoom, which is a behaviour no real browser has.

constraint: screen.width x devicePixelRatio and screen.height x devicePixelRatio must be a panel resolution the claimed hardware actually ships, in the same sense that coh.hardware-product-configuration requires a purchasable machine.

evidence.note: 1728 x 2 = 3456 and 1117 x 2 = 2234, which is the 16-inch MacBook Pro panel exactly; the logical size alone would not have shown this
bounds and backingScaleFactor are read from the same NSScreen, so the product is by construction the real panel on real hardware

notes: Catches the characteristic per-field synthesis error: a plausible logical size paired with a plausible scale factor whose product is not a display anyone manufactures. Marked strong rather than fatal because scaled display modes on macOS produce logical sizes whose product is a rendering target rather than the panel, so the check needs the profile's model to rule.

constraint: screen.orientation.type must be the landscape family when screen.width >= screen.height and the portrait family otherwise, and screen.orientation.angle must be 0 for the primary orientation of an unrotated desktop display.

evidence.note: GetOrientationTypeForDesktop classifies from `bounds.height() >= bounds.width()` and the panel rotation angle; the type is derived from the bounds, not stored beside them
1728x1117 with type landscape-primary and angle 0

notes: Free if the bounds are patched at DisplayUtil::DisplayToScreenInfo, because the type is computed from them there. Broken instantly by a patch applied only to Screen::width()/height(), which is the point of recording it.

constraint: The CSS device-width and device-height media features must equal screen.width and screen.height.

evidence.note: both read ScreenInfo::rect through ChromeClient, so in stock Chrome they are the same two integers

notes: The cheap check that catches a patch applied to the Screen accessor instead of to ScreenInfo. A few dozen matchMedia calls recover device-width by binary search without touching the screen object at all.

constraint: The window rect must lie inside the claimed available rect: screenX >= availLeft, screenY >= availTop, screenX + outerWidth <= availLeft + availWidth, and screenY + outerHeight <= availTop + availHeight. Negative screen coordinates are impossible for a single-display profile.
check: screenX >= availLeft and screenY >= availTop and screenX + outerWidth <= availLeft + availWidth and screenY + outerHeight <= availTop + availHeight

evidence.note: screenX 0 == availLeft 0, screenY 33 == availTop 33, outerHeight 1000 <= availHeight 1001, outerWidth 1728 == availWidth 1728 — the window sits flush inside the work area

the window rect and the available rect reach the renderer over two different mojo channels from two different browser-side sources, so nothing in Chromium enforces this relation once the screen values are spoofed

notes: This is why window.outer-dimensions and window.screen-position are inherit rather than spoof: the requirement is a relation the profile loader satisfies by placing and sizing the real OS window, not a value to write. It also imposes a hard usability constraint that mirrors coh.claim-within-host-capacity — a profile claiming a display smaller than the host's cannot be run maximised, and a profile claiming one larger than the host's can never fill it. The loader should clamp the launch window rather than let arithmetic that cannot hold ship.

constraint: outerHeight - innerHeight is the height of the browser's own chrome and outerWidth - innerWidth is its horizontal frame plus any classic scrollbar. Both deltas are platform-specific and must match the claimed OS.

evidence.note: outerHeight 1000 - innerHeight 913 = 87px of vertical chrome, and outerWidth 1728 - innerWidth 1728 = 0px horizontally — macOS has no window side frame and uses overlay scrollbars
outer comes from the OS window rect and inner from the layout view size, so the difference is the real browser furniture and is produced by the platform, not by any value we can set

notes: The screen-geometry analogue of coh.platform-resource-sets: a macOS profile served from a Windows host contradicts itself in this subtraction with no screen value patched at all, because Windows adds horizontal window frame and a 15-17px classic scrollbar that macOS does not have. Marked strong rather than fatal because the vertical delta legitimately varies with the bookmarks bar, extensions and downloads shelf, so only the horizontal delta and the coarse magnitude are reliable. Cheap to satisfy when host OS and claimed OS agree; not fixable inside this subsystem when they do not.

constraint: The Viewport-Width / Sec-CH-Viewport-Width header must equal window.innerWidth, and Sec-CH-Viewport-Height must equal window.innerHeight, for requests made from that document.

evidence.note: viewport-width 1728 on the wire against window.innerWidth 1728

subresource requests take the value from LocalFrameView::ViewportWidth in the renderer while navigation requests take it from view->GetVisibleViewportSize() in the browser, divided by two different zoom sources

notes: Strong rather than fatal because the navigation header is necessarily stale relative to the document it loads — it describes the viewport before layout. The check is only decisive against subresource requests, where the same process produced both numbers.

constraint: screen.isExtended false requires that getScreenDetails() enumerate exactly one screen and that the window's screen coordinates lie within that one screen's rect.
check: not screen.isExtended implies len(screenDetails.screens) == 1 and window_within(screenDetails.screens[0])

evidence.note: is_extended is GetNumDisplays() > 1 while getScreenDetails enumerates the ScreenInfos list built by GetScreenInfosNearestDisplay — the same display list, read two ways, so flipping one boolean does not shorten the other
isExtended false with screenX 0 and screenY 33, inside the single 1728x1117 screen

notes: Depends on screen.details, which is currently escalated for lack of corpus coverage, so this edge cannot close until the collector gains a getScreenDetails probe. Recorded now because it settles how screen.is-extended must be patched: shorten the ScreenInfos list, do not flip the flag.

constraint: The WebGL limit table, the twelve shader precision triples, the two extension lists and the rendered pixels are all produced by one ANGLE backend. They must therefore all be the values that the backend named by the claimed GPU produces on the claimed OS. Claiming a GPU whose only real backend differs from the one actually running contradicts every one of them simultaneously, and no per-value patch reconciles it because the pixels would still come from the running backend.
check: webgl_tables_match_backend(claimed_gpu, claimed_os, parameters, precision, extensions) and render_matches_backend(claimed_backend, canvas2d_hash, webgl_pixels_hash)

evidence.note: the limits and precisions are backend constants, not GPU queries, so they identify the backend rather than the GPU
each backend branch is guarded by a supports_angle_* flag, so backend availability is bounded by the host OS
every captured limit and precision equals the ANGLE Metal constant, confirming the table describes the backend

notes: The structural constraint of this subsystem. Its practical consequence is that profiles are partitioned by (OS, ANGLE backend) and cannot be loaded outside their partition. See the gpu.angle-backend row for the full argument and the measurement that would size the residual within-partition risk.

constraint: The applied driver-bug workaround set, the disabled-extension set and the GPU feature status must be the ones Chromium's own control lists produce for the claimed GPUInfo, not the ones they produce for the host's hardware.

evidence.note: both lists are evaluated against GPUInfo and their results merged into GpuFeatureInfo, which then reaches the renderer
253 entries keyed on vendor_id, device_id, gl_vendor, gl_renderer, driver_version and os - all GPUInfo fields
GpuFeatureInfo::disabled_webgl_extensions is read straight into the WebGL context's disabled_extensions_, making the blocklist decision page-observable

notes: Strong rather than fatal: a mismatch is only visible when the claimed GPU is one the lists actually have an entry for. But it is the cheapest correctness win in the subsystem, because setting GPUInfo once before ComputeGpuFeatureInfo makes Chromium derive the whole downstream configuration correctly for free.

constraint: The reported SAMPLES, SAMPLE_BUFFERS, MAX_SAMPLES and getContextAttributes().antialias must describe the multisample configuration that actually produced the rendered bytes. Reporting a sample count the drawing buffer was not allocated with is detectable by rendering a diagonal edge and inspecting the coverage values.

evidence.note: sample_count_ is both the reported value's source and the argument to the multisample renderbuffer allocation, so they cannot diverge unless a patch makes them

evidence.source: resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T033252Z.json probes['webgl1']: SAMPLES 4, SAMPLE_BUFFERS 1, antialiasSamples 4, antialias true; probes['webgl2']: MAX_SAMPLES 4
evidence.note: self-consistent on real hardware and identical across page loads

notes: Recorded as an edge specifically because sample count is one of the few render inputs we can legitimately set, and the temptation when setting it is to change the report without changing the allocation. Doing that turns a valid configuration change into a detectable one.

constraint: The glyphs rasterised into a canvas, the metrics measureText returns, and the installed font set enumerated elsewhere must all describe one font installation. A canvas text render that used a fallback font while the font set claims the requested font is present is a contradiction, and so is the reverse.

evidence.note: every TextMetrics field is derived from font data and shaping
the same font object supplies the SkFont used to rasterise canvas text
one host, one font installation, one set of metrics

notes: Jointly owned with subsystem 7, which owns the font set itself. Recorded from this side because canvas is where the contradiction becomes visible: a detector that measures a string and then renders it is comparing two views of the same font installation, and both must move together. This is also why canvas.measure-text should be reassigned to fonts-text.

constraint: navigator.gpu.getPreferredCanvasFormat() must be 'rgba8unorm' if and only if the claimed platform is Linux or Android, and 'bgra8unorm' otherwise.

evidence.note: the value is selected purely by BUILDFLAG(IS_ANDROID) || BUILDFLAG(IS_LINUX), with no device or driver input

notes: Fatal and free to check. It is a compile-time constant, so on a Linux host running a macOS or Windows profile it is wrong from the first frame and cannot be fixed by configuration - only by patching the branch. That makes it a concrete instance of the OS-partition argument in coh.angle-backend-vs-gpu-claim.

constraint: For identical drawing operations at identical size, an OffscreenCanvas 2D readback and an HTMLCanvasElement 2D readback should return the same bytes, in the main thread and in a worker alike, to whatever extent stock Chrome does.
check: hash(offscreen_2d_render) == hash(canvas_2d_render) for identical draw ops

evidence.note: the two acceleration decisions are independent: OffscreenCanvas has neither the small-canvas cutoff nor the willReadFrequently input, so the two paths can select different raster backends for the same drawing operations

evidence.source: a cross-scope render comparison is a standard detector technique, and a fork that changes only one of the two paths breaks it silently

notes: Deliberately weak and proposed rather than open: we do not yet know whether stock Chrome satisfies this, and asserting it would be inventing a constraint. The capture has no OffscreenCanvas probe. What would settle it: add one to the collector, run it on real hardware in worker and main-thread scope, and record whether the hashes match. If stock Chrome already differs, the edge should be dropped and the real constraint is only that we differ in the same way it does.

constraint: The font set observable through CSS family matching in the renderer, the set queryLocalFonts() returns from the browser process, and the set reachable through @font-face src:local() must all describe one installation.
check: set(css_width_probe_hits) subset_of set(queryLocalFonts().map(f => f.family)) and set(local_src_hits) == set(css_width_probe_hits)

evidence.note: BestStyleMatchForFamily calls CTFontCollectionCreateFromAvailableFonts in the RENDERER for CSS matching
FontEnumerationDataSourceMac::GetFonts makes the same CoreText call in the BROWSER, with different options and a different validity filter
the IsFontFamilyUnavailable veto covers MatchFontFamily only; MatchUniqueFont, which serves src:local(), never consults it
on Linux both the family match and the local() match are answered by FontServiceApp in the browser process, so the split falls in a different place again

document.fonts.check returns true for Segoe UI, Roboto and Noto Color Emoji while the width probe finds none of them — stock Chrome ALREADY disagrees across these APIs, so the invariant is 'reproduce stock Chrome's disagreement', not 'make them agree'

notes: The fonts instance of the multi-process pattern already found for deviceMemory, DPR and Accept-Language, and the most expensive one to get wrong because the browser-process view is a complete dump rather than a yes/no oracle. A renderer-only denylist at FontCache::MarkFontFamilyAsUnavailable produces a page where CSS sees the profile's font set and one click on queryLocalFonts() sees the host's — decisive on its own. Three enforcement points are needed, not one: the renderer family matcher, the renderer local() matcher, and FontEnumerationDataSource::GetFonts or FontEnumerationCache in the browser. The T0 line is the subtlety: FontFaceSet.check disagreeing with the width probe is CORRECT behaviour and must be preserved, so the check is not naive set equality across all four members.

constraint: Each of serif, sans-serif, monospace, cursive, fantasy and math must resolve to a family that is present in the claimed installed set, and the width of a font-detection MISS must equal the width of that resolved family.
check: all(generic_family_map[g] in fonts.installed for g in generics) and all(miss_width[g] == width_of(generic_family_map[g]) for g in generics)

evidence.note: monospace 636 == Menlo 636, sans-serif 720 == Helvetica 720, serif 692 == Times 692 — the identity holds exactly on real hardware, for all three generics, in both directions
the macOS generic map is a browser-process pref default, independently confirming the same three families
FontSelector::FamilyNameFromSettings performs the substitution, so the miss width is literally the resolved family's width and cannot drift from it

notes: This is the edge that punishes patching the font set alone. Every MISS in a detection probe returns the generic baseline byte-for-byte, so a probe over 300 families yields the generic map as a free by-product; if the set says the host is macOS while sans-serif still measures as DejaVu Sans, the contradiction is in the same JSON object the detector already collected. Cheap to satisfy: the seven ScriptFontFamilyMap prefs are already plumbed browser->renderer and need no C++ change.

constraint: Every sub-pixel width and height a page can measure must be the exact advance and metric sum of the fonts the claimed installation contains, at the font's own unitsPerEm granularity.
check: clientrect_width(s, font) == sum(advance(glyph, font) for glyph in shape(s)) and measureText(s).width == that same sum

evidence.note: 'Apostate mLj' at 24px monospace. Menlo advance 1233/2048 em; 12 * 24 * 1233/2048 = 355104/2048 = 173.390625 exactly. The client rect is the unrounded advance sum and nothing else.
= 212172/2048, the same 1/2048 granularity from the same shaping pipeline at 14px Arial
measureText sums ShapeResult::Width over the same ShapeResult layout uses, and every advance in it came from strike_ref.getWidth on the font binary

notes: The three-way coupling named in the subsystem brief, now measured rather than asserted: one wrong font shows up simultaneously in getClientRects, measureText and any canvas text render, and cannot be repaired in any of them. It also fixes the direction of dependency for the ledger — layout.client-rects and canvas.measure-text are both 'inherit' precisely BECAUSE this edge holds; they are outputs of the font set, so the only way to make them right is to make fonts.installed and fonts.generic-families right.

constraint: For one string in one font, ctx.measureText(s).width and the width of a client rect around the same shaped text must be produced by the same shaping run and must agree.

evidence.note: TextMetrics::MeasureRuns accumulates shape_result->Width() from ShapeResult objects produced by PlainTextPainter — the same shaper and the same ShapeResult type layout consumes
both report exact multiples of 1/2048 on the same host in the same page load; neither shows the 1/64 LayoutUnit quantisation that would appear if they came from different pipelines

notes: Recorded as a first-class edge because it is the cheapest tamper test a detector can run and the easiest invariant for a fork to break. Measure a string with measureText, lay the same string out and read a Range client rect, and compare. Any per-surface patch — noise in one, rounding in the other, a hook on the canvas path only — separates two numbers that stock Chrome derives from a single ShapeResult. Owned by fonts-text jointly with screen-geometry, since neither side can honour it alone.

constraint: The six CSS system-font keywords must show the pattern the claimed OS produces: six identical Arial/16px rows on macOS, Linux and ChromeOS, but a 3-and-3 split on Windows where menu, small-caption and status-bar come from NONCLIENTMETRICS while caption, icon and message-box stay Arial/16.

evidence.note: real macOS Chrome 152: all six return Arial / 16px / 400 / normal
layout_theme_font_provider_win.cc is compiled only when is_win; every other platform gets the default provider, which returns DefaultGUIFont() for all six ids
the Windows split: small-caption, menu and status-bar from FontCache metrics, the other three from DefaultGUIFont/DefaultFontSize
the Windows values originate in the browser process from gfx::win::SystemFont and arrive as RendererPreferences, so they are settable from a profile without patching Blink

notes: A one-read OS discriminator that costs a detector nothing. It only bites for cross-OS profiles: a macOS profile on a macOS or Linux build is already exactly right, because the value is a Blink constant rather than a host query. A Windows profile served from any non-Windows build returns six identical Arial rows where real Windows Chrome returns a split, and no amount of correctness elsewhere explains it. Pairs with coh.platform-resource-sets, which owns the broader 'resource sets must match the claimed OS' constraint.

constraint: The font chosen for a codepoint no requested family covers, and the advance width it contributes, must be the one the claimed OS's text engine would choose from the claimed installation.

evidence.note: 103.599609375 includes the Apple Color Emoji advance for U+1F512, so one measureText call carries a fallback observation
emoji fallback is the hard-coded constant 'Apple Color Emoji' on macOS, before CoreText is consulted
last-resort fallback is hard-coded Times then Lucida Grande

on Linux the emoji codepoint is rewritten to U+1F46A and the choice is made by fontconfig in the browser process, returning a filepath rather than a family name — a structurally different answer, not merely a different font

notes: The hardest edge in the subsystem and the reason fonts.fallback-font is escalated. Fallback advances come out of a font binary that is either on the host or is not, so a Linux host claiming macOS cannot produce Apple Color Emoji metrics by any patch. Note also that the macOS character-fallback cache (font_cache_mac.mm:326-341) is documented as introducing context sensitivity for ideographic codepoints, so repeated probes are not guaranteed independent — which interacts with coh.render-determinism and should be measured before either row is closed.

constraint: Integer ascent and descent, and the line heights derived from them, must be produced by the rounding path the claimed OS's build uses — Skia rounding alone on macOS and Windows, VDMX bytecode metrics plus the descent-borrow adjustment on Linux, ChromeOS and Android.

evidence.note: the VDMX table is parsed and its ascent/descent used in place of Skia's ONLY under IS_LINUX||IS_CHROMEOS||IS_ANDROID||IS_FUCHSIA, and only when hinting is full or normal; the comment states CoreText and DirectWrite never bytecode-hint
a second Linux/ChromeOS/Android-only branch moves one unit from ascent to descent when the descent rounded down and subpixel positioning is on
fontBoundingBoxAscent 13 and Descent 3 are integers beside a fractional width in the same object — the macOS signature of Skia rounding with no VDMX path

notes: A build-flag divergence rather than a value, which makes it unusual in this ledger: no profile field can carry it, because the branch is chosen at compile time by the target OS. Even with the exact macOS font files installed, a Linux build could report different integer ascent and descent for the same font at the same size, and that propagates into every line height in the document via SimpleFontData::PlatformInit:175. Whether the two branches actually change the numbers for common fonts is measurable and currently unmeasured; one Linux capture with the existing collector settles it, and the answer determines whether cross-OS profiles are viable at all.

constraint: Whether glyph advances are exact font-unit fractions or rounded integers must be the same everywhere in a session and must match the claimed platform: always fractional on macOS, host-configured on Linux and Windows.

evidence.note: `if (!subpixel) sk_width = SkScalarRoundToInt(sk_width)` — one boolean quantises every advance in the browser
should_subpixel_position is hard-coded true on macOS outside web tests, and drives both setSubpixel and setLinearMetrics
on Linux and Windows the equivalent flags arrive from the browser process as RendererPreferences, derived from the host's fontconfig and desktop settings
every text-driven value in the capture is fractional at 1/2048 granularity, consistent with subpixel positioning on

notes: A host leak with an unusually wide blast radius: the same flag decides advance quantisation (skia_text_metrics.cc:32), the descent-borrow in font_metrics.cc:121-130, and canvas glyph rasterisation via the SkFont, so a mismatched host setting contradicts a macOS claim in getClientRects, measureText and the canvas pixel buffer at once. The fix is not a Blink patch but a profile-loader one — set the RendererPreferences font fields from the profile instead of from the host — which is why this edge is proposed jointly with subsystem 1.

constraint: navigator.storage.estimate().quota must equal usage + 10 GiB exactly. Any other value means either the partition volume is smaller than 10 GiB or the profile is off-the-record.

evidence.note: CalculateReportedQuota has exactly two branches and both are deterministic; there is no path that produces a value between ceil(total) and 10 GiB other than a small volume or the incognito capacity substitution
quota 10737418240 with usage 0 on a real headed Chrome 152

notes: A one-line equality that catches three different failure modes at once: a container with a volume under 10 GiB, an off-the-record profile, and any tool that writes a plausible disk-derived number into quota because it is working from pre-M110 knowledge. Strong rather than fatal only because a genuinely small volume is a real if unusual configuration; on a profile claiming a laptop or desktop it is decisive.

constraint: quota minus usage is invariant across reads within a session; writing N bytes must raise both usage and quota by the same amount.

evidence.note: both return branches are `clamped_usage_bytes + <constant>`, so the difference is fixed and the page can force a re-read after a known write

notes: The active version of the previous edge: a detector does not have to accept the first answer, it can write a megabyte to IndexedDB and re-read. A replayed literal quota fails immediately; the real implementation cannot. This is the specific reason storage.estimate-quota must be inherited rather than pinned to a captured constant.

constraint: A default storage bucket's estimate().quota must equal navigator.storage.estimate().quota; a bucket opened with an explicit quota must report that exact number instead.

evidence.note: the bucket path reaches the same CalculateReportedQuota, except that a bucket with bucket.quota > 0 short-circuits and echoes the requested value verbatim

notes: A second, less obvious read of the same browser-side number. Any tool that intercepts navigator.storage.estimate but not the Storage Buckets API - which is most of them, the API being recent - reports two different quotas for the same origin in the same document.

constraint: In a secure top-level same-origin context, Notification.permission and navigator.permissions.query({name:'notifications'}).state must name the same state under the mapping default<->prompt, granted<->granted, denied<->denied.

evidence.note: __NotificationPermission 'default' and notifications 'prompt' in one read on real headed Chrome

the only divergence in the tree: a BrowserContext with no PlatformNotificationService returns DENIED without consulting the permission controller, which is exactly what chrome-headless-shell does while its permission manager keeps saying ASK

the two legitimate exceptions - insecure contexts and frames cross-origin to the outermost main frame - which is why the constraint is scoped to a secure top-level same-origin context rather than stated unconditionally

notes: The edge named in docs/SUBSYSTEMS.md section 11. It is fatal because there is no legitimate configuration of a headed Chrome in which the two disagree in a top-level secure context, and because the check costs a detector two property reads. It is also not fixable inside this subsystem: the cause is which BrowserContext implementation the binary was built with, which makes it a profile-loader and build-variant constraint.

constraint: On a fresh profile, background-sync, clipboard-write, accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, screen-wake-lock and payment-handler must all read 'granted', and geolocation, notifications, camera, microphone, midi, persistent-storage and clipboard-read must all read 'prompt'.

evidence.note: the fourteen-name map measured on real headed Chrome 152 / macOS, seven granted and seven prompt
the failure mode: ASK for every permission unconditionally, which flips all seven granted names to 'prompt' simultaneously
the five independent sources that produce the seven granted values, three registry defaults and two hard overrides

notes: A wider and more robust headless check than the Notification one, because it does not depend on a single property and cannot be satisfied by patching one value: seven names move together and they are produced by five different pieces of browser-process code. Recorded here so that the requirement is visible to whoever chooses the base binary. Nothing to patch on a headed build - the whole map comes out right by itself.

constraint: navigator.permissions.query({name:'keyboard-lock'}) and {name:'pointer-lock'} must resolve on a profile claiming a desktop OS and must throw a TypeError on one claiming Android or iOS.

evidence.note: both cases are wrapped in #if !BUILDFLAG(IS_ANDROID) && !BUILDFLAG(IS_IOS) and throw "The Keyboard Lock permission isn't available on this platform." otherwise

notes: A compile-time platform assertion reachable from JavaScript through a permission query, which is not where anyone looks for one. It cannot be satisfied by any runtime patch on a desktop build claiming Android - the branch is not there to disable - so it belongs on the list of reasons a mobile profile needs a mobile build rather than a mobile user agent.

constraint: await navigator.storage.persisted() must be true exactly when navigator.permissions.query({name:'persistent-storage'}).state is 'granted'.

evidence.note: persisted() is PermissionService::HasPermission(PERSISTENT_STORAGE) resolved as status == GRANTED - one bit, two APIs, no intermediate state
the pair agreeing in a single capture

notes: The storage analogue of the Notification edge, and the same lesson: a value that looks like a storage property is a permission read, so a tool that models the two subsystems separately can make them contradict each other. Nothing to do on stock code.

constraint: accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer must always report the same permission state as each other, and DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission() must resolve to that same state.
check: len(set(states['accelerometer'], states['gyroscope'], states['magnetometer'])) == 1 and device_orientation_request_permission() == states['accelerometer']

evidence.note: all three names fall through to CreatePermissionDescriptor(PermissionName::SENSORS) in one case block, so they are one bit
requestPermission() requests the same PermissionName::SENSORS
accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer all 'granted' in one read

notes: Four observables, one browser-side bit. Cheap for a detector to check and easy for a value-by-value spoof to break, since the four are reached through three different APIs (Permissions, the Sensor constructors, the DeviceOrientationEvent static) and nothing in the JavaScript surface suggests they are the same permission.

constraint: A profile claiming macOS must expose Accelerometer and Gyroscope, must not expose Magnetometer or AmbientLightSensor, must report the sensor permission as granted, and must nevertheless fail every start() with a NotReadableError and never fire a deviceorientation event.

evidence.note: CreateSensorInternal runs the callback with nullptr for every type, so no macOS Chrome can produce a reading
that nullptr becomes NotReadableError rather than NotAllowedError, which is how a detector tells 'no hardware' from 'permission refused'
interfaces present, permission granted, on hardware where the sensor can never start

notes: The interesting shape is the contradiction that is correct: permission granted, interface present, sensor permanently unavailable. It is a positive macOS signature rather than an absence, so it can be checked in both directions - and a Windows or Android host with real sensors serving a macOS profile fails it by succeeding. Open rather than resolved because the collector has no start() probe, so the second half of the constraint is unmeasured.

constraint: getBattery() returning exactly {charging: true, level: 1, chargingTime: 0, dischargingTime: Infinity} means no battery hardware, which is correct for a desktop and wrong for a profile claiming a laptop. Whenever a battery exists, exactly one of chargingTime and dischargingTime is finite and the finite one is a multiple of 60.

evidence.note: the struct defaults are precisely that tuple, and a platform with no BatteryStatusManager never overwrites them
chargingTime and dischargingTime are base::Minutes(k).InSeconds() and are Infinity when the platform cannot estimate, so a non-multiple of 60 is a value Chromium cannot emit
charging true, level 0.24, chargingTime 5160 (= 86 minutes), dischargingTime Infinity on a real charging MacBook

notes: The edge that turns battery from device state into a coherence constraint. It is satisfiable for free by pairing desktop profiles with battery-less hosts, which is why battery.status is escalated to a profile decision rather than opened as a patch. The multiple-of-60 invariant is worth keeping in view separately: it is a cheap way to catch any tool that synthesises a chargingTime, since a randomised value is almost never divisible by 60.

constraint: navigator.mimeTypes.length is 2 exactly when navigator.plugins.length is 5 and 0 exactly when it is 0, and navigator.mimeTypes[0].enabledPlugin must be the same object as navigator.plugins[0].

evidence.note: GetFixedMimeTypeArray hands back plugins[0]'s own DOMMimeType members, so the two arrays share objects rather than values, and a DCHECK asserts plugins[0] has exactly two mime types
five plugins and two mime types with matching fields

notes: Object identity, not structural equality - which is what makes it useful. Any spoof that builds navigator.plugins and navigator.mimeTypes as two independent arrays, as every JavaScript-level implementation must, fails a single === . Extends the existing coh.pdf-viewer-vs-plugin-list edge from two observables to three.

constraint: The 38 system colours must be the table Chromium generates for the claimed OS at the reported prefers-color-scheme and forced-colors values - the generic constants plus the macOS Highlight pair on macOS, GetSysColor-derived values on Windows in light mode, and one of the five named palettes only when forced-colors is active.

evidence.note: three different per-platform implementations of MapNativeColorsToCssSystemColors - two colours hard-coded on macOS, ten OS-derived on Windows in light mode, an empty stub on Linux - so the table differs by host platform even before the claim is considered
AddCssSystemColorMixer replaces the entire table with one of five literal palettes when forced_colors is not kNone, so forced-colors and the colour map must agree
the dark-mode table measured alongside prefers-color-scheme: dark and forced-colors: none

notes: Fatal because a single getComputedStyle read can contradict the claimed OS with no screen, GPU or font value involved, and because the mismatch is systematic rather than marginal - the Linux stub gives Highlight rgb(25,103,210) where macOS gives rgba(179,215,255,0.8). Pairs with coh.platform-resource-sets, which binds this to fonts, voices and system fonts as one fact with four faces; this edge adds the intra-surface constraint that the table must also agree with the reported colour scheme and forced-colors state.

constraint: The single voice with default true must be a plausible system default for the profile's locale, and the voice list's language coverage must include the languages the profile claims.

evidence.note: the platform default voice is hoisted to index 0 and index 0 is what becomes is_default, so the default entry is the user's configured system voice rather than an arbitrary one
Samantha, en-US, default true, on a machine whose captured navigator.languages leads with en-US

notes: Weak because the relation is a plausibility judgement rather than an equality - a user can set an en-GB system voice on a machine running in French, and many do. It is recorded so that a replayed voice list is not paired with an unrelated locale, which is the realistic failure when voice lists and language settings come from different profile sources.

constraint: The rendered float samples are produced by an FFT kernel chosen at runtime from the host CPU's feature bits (AVX+FMA, SSE, NEON, scalar) and by an oscillator kernel chosen at compile time from the target architecture. A profile's audio render is only reproducible on a host in the same ISA class, and the architecture the profile claims must be the architecture whose kernels the binary actually runs.

evidence.note: runtime CPU feature detection selects the kernel
AVX fuses the multiply-add, SSE does not - the kernels are not arithmetically equivalent
three separate oscillator kernels compiled per target CPU, whose own comments document differing round-off

notes: Severity is strong rather than fatal only because we have not yet MEASURED the size of the difference - see the escalation in audio.offline-render for the exact captures that would settle it. If they show a differing hash, this becomes fatal and profiles must be partitioned by ISA class the way gpu.angle-backend partitions them by ANGLE backend.

constraint: The compressor and the decibel conversions call sin, exp, powf and log10f unqualified, so the render embeds the host operating system's libm. A profile claiming one OS while running on another cannot produce that OS's samples.

evidence.note: bare sin() and exp() in a file that otherwise uses fdlibm
bare powf and log10f on the compressor's per-sample metering path, with no double-to-float truncation to absorb a last-ULP difference
and when WebAudioRustFft is disabled the FFT itself becomes Apple Accelerate on Mac and PFFFT elsewhere, which is an outright different transform rather than a last-ULP difference

notes: This edge and coh.audio-render-vs-host-cpu-isa together are the audio statement of the same structural fact gpu.angle-backend records for graphics: the render identifies the platform the code is running on, not the device the profile claims. They are separate edges because the two terms are separable by experiment - an Intel Mac isolates the libm term, an AVX-masked Linux box isolates the ISA term.

constraint: The OfflineAudioContext render must not change when the claimed audio hardware changes. Its sample rate, length and channel count are constructor arguments and nothing on that path reads a device, so a fork in which spoofing AudioContext.sampleRate alters the offline render hash has introduced a coupling that stock Chrome does not have.
check: render_hash(profile_A) == render_hash(profile_B) whenever profile_A and profile_B differ only in audio.sample_rate, audio.frames_per_buffer or audio.max_channel_count

evidence.note: the offline sample rate is the constructor argument, validated and used verbatim
MaxChannelCount returns the constructor's channel count, not the hardware's

evidence.source: resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T083721Z.json - probes['audio.offline_render'].sampleRate is 44100 while probes['audio.properties'].sampleRate is 48000 on the same machine in the same page load
evidence.note: stock Chrome already demonstrates the independence: the offline context runs at the requested 44100 while the hardware context runs at 48000

notes: Fatal because it is a one-line detector: request an OfflineAudioContext at a rate the claimed hardware does not support and check that the render still happens and still hashes the same. A naive patch that routes the offline destination through the spoofed hardware parameters fails this immediately, and it is the most likely wrong turn on this shard.

constraint: baseLatency * sampleRate must equal max(hardware frames_per_buffer, 128) exactly - an integer, and on every platform we have seen a power of two within the platform's [kMinAudioBufferSize, kMaxAudioBufferSize] range.
check: round(fp['audio.properties'].baseLatency * fp['audio.properties'].sampleRate) == profile.audio.frames_per_buffer and is_power_of_two(profile.audio.frames_per_buffer) and profile.audio.frames_per_buffer >= 128

evidence.note: base_latency_ = max(GetFramesPerBuffer(), renderQuantumSize()) / sampleRate() - the relation is exact by construction
and 256 = 2 * media::limits::kMinAudioBufferSize on macOS

notes: Fatal and free to check. Spoofing sampleRate without moving frames_per_buffer produces a baseLatency whose product is not an integer, which is a one-multiplication tell. This is the audio analogue of coh.dpr-times-screen-is-real-panel.

constraint: The audio hardware parameter set - sample rate, buffer size, output channel count and the device counts - must be jointly plausible for the claimed operating system and machine class. All four are produced together by one AudioManager implementation in the audio service, so they cannot be chosen independently.

evidence.note: GetPreferredOutputStreamParameters emits the sample rate, channel layout and buffer size as one AudioParameters object; they are not independent values

evidence.source: resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T083721Z.json - 48000 Hz, 256 frames, 2 channels, one device of each kind
evidence.note: the macOS laptop tuple

evidence.source: resources/surfaces.json, category audio: "44100 on Linux defaults, 48000 on macOS" and "baseLatency ... 0.01160997... on Linux/44.1kHz"
evidence.note: a prior for what the Linux tuple looks like; it opens this edge but cannot close it, and the corpus holds no Linux row

notes: Cannot close without a second-OS capture. The prior says a Linux row is roughly (44100, 512 or 1024, 2), which would make baseLatency 0.0116099... - but that is a forum-grade number and the methodology forbids closing on it. Recorded so the corpus gap is visible rather than assumed away.

constraint: outputLatency is a reading of a live output stream. A suspended AudioContext has no stream, so a non-zero outputLatency on a context reporting state 'suspended' is incoherent. Separately, the quantization granularity of outputLatency (8 ms versus 1 ms) must match the microphone permission state the Permissions API reports.
check: not (fp['audio.properties'].state == 'suspended' and fp['audio.properties'].outputLatency != 0) and quantum_of(outputLatency) == (0.001 if mic_permission == 'granted' else 0.008)

evidence.note: the quantizing factor is chosen by a PermissionName::AUDIO_CAPTURE check performed at construction (:685-690)
so a running context can legitimately read 0; only the converse direction is constrained

notes: Weak on its own, and recorded mainly for the permission link: the granularity of a latency number is an oblique read of a permission state, which is the kind of cross-API inference that only shows up when two subsystems are patched by different owners. Jointly relevant to subsystem 11.

constraint: The Web Audio node defaults and ranges and the getSupportedConstraints key set are compile-time Blink constants. They must be exactly those of the Chromium version the user agent claims - no extra keys from a flipped RuntimeEnabledFeature, no missing ones.

evidence.note: the [RuntimeEnabled=MediaCaptureBackgroundBlur] and [RuntimeEnabled=MediaCaptureCameraControls] members are present or absent purely by feature flag

evidence.source: resources/fingerprints/raw/apple-m4-max-20260907T083721Z.json - 35 constraint keys, with backgroundBlur, backgroundSegmentationMask, eyeGazeCorrection and faceFraming absent
evidence.note: a direct readout of which Blink features are enabled in stock Chrome 152

notes: This is the cheapest regression check on the whole shard and it catches a whole class of self-inflicted wounds: any --enable-blink-features or --disable-blink-features we add for another subsystem that happens to touch a capture or audio feature shows up here as a set difference against the corpus. Worth wiring into V3 as an exact set comparison rather than a spot check.

constraint: Both reads are driven by the same FFTFrame instance selection and the same host libm, so they must move together. A browser whose offline render matches the corpus but whose analyser spectrum does not has patched one and not the other.
check: both surfaces match the same corpus row, or neither does

evidence.note: both call into FFTFrame, which is a single dispatcher over one backend selection
LinearToDecibels is shared between the analyser's per-bin conversion and the compressor's metering

notes: Opened rather than resolved because audio.analyser-frequency-data has no corpus row at all. The edge exists to stop the analyser being forgotten once the offline render is dealt with - it is the same machinery with two extra libm calls and no float truncation, so it is strictly the easier of the two to get wrong.

constraint: The codec support table is compiled per operating system - HEVC, the OS software encoders and several profile gates are constexpr BUILDFLAG(IS_MAC) / IS_WIN / IS_ANDROID. The codec answers a profile gives must be the answers a binary built for the claimed OS gives.

evidence.note: constexpr OS branches - a Mac binary cannot answer as a Windows one
the macOS answer set, including hev1 supported and powerEfficient

notes: Same shape as coh.preferred-canvas-format-vs-os and coh.angle-backend-vs-gpu-claim: an OS claim that the host binary cannot back. It reinforces the partition-by-OS conclusion the GPU shard reached, from an independent surface, which is worth stating because it means the partition is not a graphics-specific inconvenience but a property of the fork.

constraint: A browser claiming to be Chrome must be built with Chrome's media build flags. With proprietary_codecs=false or ffmpeg_branding!=Chrome, every avc1, mp4a and HEVC answer flips to the empty string while the user agent still says Chrome.

evidence.note: the whole H.264 and AAC block is inside #if !BUILDFLAG(USE_PROPRIETARY_CODECS) negation
stock Chrome's answer, and the value our build must reproduce

notes: A build-configuration gate, not a patch, but it belongs in the ledger because it is invisible until someone runs the collector against our own binary and it invalidates every other row at once. It is the single cheapest V2 smoke check on this shard: two canPlayType calls.

constraint: The WebRTC sender and receiver video codec lists, their ordering, their profile and level parameters, and mediaCapabilities' powerEfficient flag are all derived from the same GPU-process hardware encoder and decoder enumeration that the claimed GPU implies. They must describe the GPU the profile claims, not the host's.

evidence.source: net/socket/socks5_client_socket.cc:31 and net/base/proxy_server.h, as established by subsystem 10
evidence.note: Chromium's SOCKS5 implements only kTunnelCommand = 0x01. There is no UDP ASSOCIATE and no ProxyDatagramClientSocket anywhere in net/socket. So the question 'what does WebRTC do about UDP when SOCKS5 is configured' has a definite answer: nothing is attempted, nothing falls back to TCP, and nothing fails - the datagram simply leaves on the host's default route.

libwebrtc's own comment asserts that binding to the ANY address reuses 'the same routing for http traffic by OS' and thereby avoids public IP leakage. That reasoning holds when HTTP goes direct and fails exactly when HTTP goes through a proxy, which is the configuration this project always runs in.

Corroborating, and independent of any page: the network service opens a UDP socket to 8.8.8.8:53 on every network change purely to read its own local address. That connect is also unproxied, so even a session in which no page ever calls RTCPeerConnection performs an unproxied outbound UDP connect to a Google address.

notes: THE HEADLINE FINDING OF THIS SHARD, and it is a deanonymisation rather than a fingerprint mismatch, so it is fatal on its own. Concretely: with --proxy-server=socks5://host:port, a page that constructs an RTCPeerConnection with any public STUN server learns the machine's real public IP address, because the STUN binding request is sent from an unproxied UDP socket in the network service and the reflexive address it returns is emitted verbatim as an srflx candidate. Neither mDNS nor any of the four IP handling modes except disable_non_proxied_udp prevents it, and the default mode is the one that permits it. The failure is not partial: it is not 'falls back to TCP' and it is not 'fails closed'; it goes direct. Jointly owned with subsystem 10, and it is the same piece of work - the SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE datagram transport designed there for QUIC is the transport this needs, substituted at services/network/p2p/socket_udp.cc rather than at net/quic/quic_session_pool.cc. Until that exists the only leak-free posture is disable_non_proxied_udp, which is itself a class-level tell recorded in coh.webrtc-candidate-set-vs-stock-default, so this edge cannot be closed by configuration alone. Note the edge names network.exit-ip-geo, which subsystem 10 owns and has not yet defined; it is already referenced by the existing coh.webrtc-network-position and should be defined once, there.

notes: This edge exists because mDNS is routinely mistaken for a complete mitigation and it is not. Cheap to enforce as a V0 lint over chrome/VERSION, DEPS and uvernum.h.
